stem: Where did the ceremonies for Nelson Mandela's inauguration on 10 May 1994 take place?
options: The Parliament building in Cape Town
The Union Buildings amphitheatre in Pretoria
A crowded football stadium in Johannesburg
The old prison grounds on Robben Island
explanation: Correct option: (B). Mandela writes that the ceremonies took place in the lovely sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria. Cape Town, a Johannesburg stadium and Robben Island are places linked with South Africa or with Mandela's life, but none of them was the site of the inauguration in the text.

stem: At the inauguration, who was sworn in as the first deputy president?

Walter Sisulu

stem: "For decades this had been the seat of white supremacy, and now it was the site of a rainbow gathering of different colours and nations." What does this contrast highlight?
options: The Union Buildings had been freshly repainted in rainbow colours
A former centre of racial rule now hosted a gathering of all races
White leaders were now excluded from the place they once ruled from
Foreign nations had at last taken control of the Union Buildings
explanation: Correct option: (B). The Union Buildings had been the centre of white rule under apartheid; on 10 May 1994 the same place hosted people of different colours and nations for the installation of the first democratic, non-racial government. 'Rainbow' is a metaphor for many peoples coming together, not literal paint. White leaders such as Mr de Klerk were part of the ceremony, so they were not excluded, and foreign leaders were guests, not rulers.

stem: In his address, Mandela speaks of "an extraordinary human disaster that lasted too long". What is he referring to?
options: the long war fought between the British and the Boers
the famines and poverty that struck rural South Africa
the long years Mandela himself spent in prison
the decades of apartheid and racial oppression
explanation: Correct option: (D). The 'human disaster' is apartheid, the system of racial domination that oppressed the dark-skinned people of South Africa for decades; out of it, he says, a society must be born of which all humanity will be proud. The Anglo-Boer war is mentioned only as background, poverty is something he pledges to fight in the future, and his imprisonment was a personal hardship rather than the national disaster he describes.

stem:
Assertion (A): In his address, Mandela says that people "who were outlaws not so long ago" had been given the rare privilege of hosting the nations of the world.
Reason (R): Because of its policy of apartheid, many countries had earlier broken off diplomatic relations with South Africa.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
explanation: Correct option: (A). Both statements are true. South Africa had been treated as an outlaw nation: many countries had cut off diplomatic relations with it because of apartheid. That is exactly why it was a rare privilege for the new democratic South Africa to host leaders from all over the world, so the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. The other options are wrong because both statements are true and directly linked.

stem: What did the highest generals of the South African defence force and police do at the inauguration?

stem: Mandela calls the air show "a demonstration of the military's loyalty to democracy". Why was this significant?
options: The air force had never before flown jets in such perfect formation
The military wanted to warn the foreign guests of South Africa's strength
Forces that once would have arrested him now served his elected government
The jets had been lent by friendly nations to honour the new government
explanation: Correct option: (C). Mandela notes that not so many years before, the same generals would have arrested him instead of saluting him. The fly-past by South African jets therefore showed that the armed forces now accepted a freely and fairly elected government. The text says nothing about a first-ever formation, a warning to guests or borrowed jets; the jets were South African.

stem: "Although that day neither group knew the lyrics of the anthem they once despised, they would soon know the words by heart." What does this sentence suggest?

Neither group was truly interested in the new government's ideals

explanation: Correct option: (D). Each group was singing an anthem it had once despised. Mandela's hope that they would soon know the words by heart shows his belief that the old hatred would turn into acceptance and unity. He mentions no law or school programme, and the willing singing shows interest in, not indifference to, the new nation.

stem:
Assertion (A): Mandela says he "was not unmindful of the fact" that, not so many years before, the generals who saluted him would have arrested him.
Reason (R): The generals saluted Mandela only because the foreign leaders present ordered them to do so.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
explanation: Correct option: (C). The Assertion is true: Mandela was well aware that the same officers would once have arrested him. The Reason is false: the text presents the salute and the air show as the military's own loyalty to a freely and fairly elected democratic government, and foreign leaders gave no orders to South Africa's forces. So the options in which the Reason is true do not apply.

stem: Based on the extract, why does Mandela believe that people can be taught to love?
options: Hatred is learnt, and love comes more naturally to the human heart
Love is required by the laws of every civil and humane society
Prison guards were always kind and gentle towards the prisoners

explanation: Correct option: (A). The extract says no one is born hating; people must learn to hate, and if they can learn to hate they can be taught to love, because love comes more naturally to the human heart. explanation: Correct option: (D). stem: "Perhaps it requires such depths of oppression to create such heights of character." Which statement best evaluates this idea from the text?
options: Oppression is desirable, since it always produces great leaders
Only nations rich in minerals can develop people of character
Great leaders are born great, so oppression has no effect on them
Severe oppression tested people and brought out rare courage
explanation: Correct option: (D). Mandela calls the rise of men like Oliver Tambo and Walter Sisulu an 'unintended' effect of decades of oppression and brutality: extreme suffering drew out extraordinary courage, wisdom and generosity. He never calls oppression desirable; he says apartheid left a deep and lasting wound. Minerals are mentioned only to say people are the greater wealth, and his point that oppression shaped these men contradicts the idea that it had no effect.

stem: Which of these is one of the "transitory freedoms" that Mandela wanted as a student?
options: the freedom of earning his own keep
the freedom of all his people to live with dignity
the freedom to marry and raise a family
the freedom to read whatever he pleased
explanation: Correct option: (D). As a student he wanted the transitory (not permanent) freedoms of staying out at night, reading what he pleased and going where he chose. Earning his keep and marrying were the 'basic and honourable freedoms' he wanted later as a young man in Johannesburg, and the freedom of his people became his goal only after he joined the ANC.

stem: Why was it almost impossible for a man of Mandela's birth and colour to fulfil both his obligations in South Africa?
options: Serving his people meant being torn from his family and home
His busy law practice left him no time for his family or people
His family refused to support his work for the African National Congress
The customs of his tribe forbade him from taking part in politics
explanation: Correct option: (A). Mandela explains that a man who tried to fulfil his duty to his people was inevitably ripped from his family and home and forced into a twilight existence of secrecy and rebellion. The text does not blame his law practice, his family's attitude or tribal customs; the cause was the apartheid system itself.

stem:
Assertion (A): Mandela says that he was not born with a hunger to be free.
Reason (R): As a boy he felt free in every way he could know, and only later discovered that his boyhood freedom was an illusion.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
explanation: Correct option: (A). Both statements are true. Mandela felt free as a boy, running in the fields and swimming in the stream, so he had no reason to hunger for freedom. The hunger began only when he learnt that this freedom was an illusion and had already been taken from him. The Reason therefore explains the Assertion; the other options either deny a true statement or the link between them.

stem: In the extract, the statement "Freedom is indivisible" means that
options: freedom can be shared only among a chosen few

stem: Which situation best reflects Mandela's idea that "the chains on any one of my people were the chains on all of them"?
options: A man enjoys privileges while his neighbours are denied basic rights
A citizen feels unfree while others in her community lack rights
A leader is released from prison and leaves public life forever
A family moves abroad to escape the unfair laws of its country
explanation: Correct option: (B). Mandela could not enjoy even his own limited freedoms while his people were not free; the citizen who feels unfree because others are denied rights shares this view. Enjoying privileges while others suffer is the opposite attitude, and withdrawing from public life or escaping abroad looks after only oneself rather than seeing one's freedom as tied to everyone else's.

stem:
Assertion (A): Mandela says he is no more virtuous or self-sacrificing than the next man.
Reason (R): From the very beginning, Mandela deliberately chose to place his people above his family.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
explanation: Correct option: (C). The Assertion is true: Mandela says he is no more virtuous than the next man, but he could not enjoy his limited freedoms while his people were not free. The Reason is false: he states, 'I did not in the beginning choose to place my people above my family'; in trying to serve his people he found he was prevented from fulfilling his duties to his family. So the options that treat the Reason as true are wrong.

stem: "It was this desire for the freedom of my people ... that transformed a frightened young man into a bold one, that drove a law-abiding attorney to become a criminal, that turned a family-loving husband into a man without a home." What is the main effect of this series of contrasts?
options: It proves that Mandela deeply regretted ever joining the ANC
It suggests that most lawyers in South Africa became criminals
It reveals that Mandela had always been a bold and lawless man
It shows how the cause of freedom reshaped his whole life
explanation: Correct option: (D). Each balanced pair sets what Mandela was before against what the struggle made him, showing that the desire for his people's freedom changed every part of his life. 'Criminal' is ironic: under apartheid laws, fighting for freedom was a crime. He expresses no regret, says nothing about other lawyers, and the contrast with a 'frightened young man' and a 'law-abiding attorney' rules out his having always been bold and lawless.
